extracted.intended_audience: school administrators, Title IX coordinators, higher-education legal counsel, recipients of federal education funds, and stakeholders submitting or reading notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of regulatory standards and interpretive guidance from the Department's preamble regarding remedial action (§106.3) and constitutional/FERPA saving clauses (§106.6(d), §106.45) in the final Title IX regulations. Focuses on what remedies OCR may require, how monetary damages are treated, and how constitutional and FERPA protections interact with Title IX enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial action limited to equitable relief consistent with 20 U.S.C. 1682
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department may require a recipient to take remedial action for discriminating in violation of Title IX or for violating Title IX implementing regulations; remedial action must be consistent with the Title IX statute at 20 U.S.C. 1682.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final §106.3(a) was revised to remove reference to assessment of damages and to clarify the Department's authority to require remedial action consistent with the statute. The preamble explains this change in response to commenters and frames remedial actions as the focus of OCR's administrative enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: OCR will not assess monetary damages administratively; courts handle monetary damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department removed references to 'assessment of damages' from §106.3(a); parties seeking monetary damages may avail themselves of the courts, which are better equipped than OCR to assess damages such as emotional distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters argued about inconsistency with prior guidance and DOJ materials; Department responded that removing 'assessment of damages' avoids confusion and does not preclude equitable payments (e.g., reimbursement) where necessary to remediate discrimination. The preamble clarifies there is no conflict between the final rule and other agencies subject to the same statutory provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on remedial actions, not punitive actions against individual perpetrators
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations are focused on remedial actions the recipient must take, rather than on punitive actions against individuals who perpetrate sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department leaves disciplinary sanctions and punitive consequences to the sound discretion of the recipient; nothing in the final regs precludes recipients from barring a respondent from enrollment or noting conduct on transcripts, but OCR's enforcement focuses on bringing recipients into compliance and securing equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients must adopt and publish grievance procedures addressing sexual harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 1975, Department regulations have required recipients to adopt and publish grievance procedures to address student and employee complaints of sex discrimination; through guidance since 1997 that requirement has been applied to complaints of sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explains that requiring grievance processes prevents recipients from violating Title IX by failing to provide remedies to victims; OCR may require recipients to investigate and adjudicate sexual harassment allegations to determine whether remedies are necessary to restore or preserve equal educational access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to recipient disciplinary decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department and courts will 'refrain from second guessing the disciplinary decisions made by school administrators' because school administrators are best positioned to determine appropriate discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While OCR enforces compliance obligations, the preamble emphasizes judicial and agency deference to institutional disciplinary decisions and reiterates that the final regulations remove 'assessment of damages' and do not attempt to micromanage institutions' sanctioning choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.6(d)(1) First Amendment saving clause: regulations do not require restriction of First Amendment rights
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.6(d)(1) states that nothing in regulations implementing Title IX requires a recipient to infringe upon any individual's rights protected under the First Amendment, including speech, expression, and academic freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble explains the clause's purpose is to avoid chilling free speech and academic freedom, to clarify the interaction of Title IX with First Amendment law, to apply to private and public recipients alike, and to note that the Department will abide by courts' rulings as to the scope of the First Amendment. The Department declined to explicitly name 'academic freedom' but indicates the clause covers it.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.6(d)(2) Due Process saving clause: regulations do not require infringement of due process; protect notice and opportunity to respond
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.6(d)(2) clarifies that nothing in the Title IX regulations requires a recipient to infringe upon any individual's rights protected under the Due Process Clauses of the Fifth or Fourteenth Amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble links these protections to procedural safeguards (notice and meaningful opportunity to respond), cites Executive Order 13563 (plain language/clarity), and refers to provisions such as §106.45(b)(5)(vi) (access to evidence) and §106.45(b)(5)(iv) (advisor of choice) as consistent with protecting due process, including for employee-respondents at private institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.6(d)(3) Other Constitutional Rights saving clause: regulations do not require infringement of other constitutional rights
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.6(d)(3) is a catch-all saving clause clarifying that nothing in regulations implementing Title IX requires a recipient to infringe upon any other rights guaranteed against government action by the U.S. Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains this provision ensures Title IX enforcement is consistent with the entire Constitution and that including a broad clause avoids implying fault by recipients while helping ensure constitutional rights are properly respected in enforcement efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: FERPA does not override federally protected due process rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department will not administer, enforce, or interpret statutes including Title IX and FERPA in a manner that would require a recipient to deny parties their constitutional due process rights; FERPA does not override federally protected due process rights of persons accused of sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble cites prior Department guidance (2001) and Supreme Court precedents (Peterson v. City of Greenville; Truax v. Raich) to explain that the Department cannot compel private entities to violate constitutional protections. The Department reiterates that parties, including employee-respondents, must have access to evidence and advisors despite FERPA concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX enforces obligations of recipients, not a direct bar against individual perpetrators; remedies target recipients' compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX applies to recipients of Federal financial assistance operating education programs or activities; it requires recipients to operate programs free from sex discrimination rather than directly barring individual respondents from perpetrating sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a recipient knowingly refuses to respond to sexual harassment, that failure is a violation of Title IX. OCR's enforcement tools include requiring remedial actions or terminating federal financial assistance to recipients, not imposing direct federal punishment on individual respondents (except insofar as recipients choose sanctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative action provision (§106.3(b)) remains unchanged
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments requesting elimination of a recipient's ability to engage in affirmative action absent a finding of violation referenced the proposed rules' decision not to alter 34 CFR 106.3(b); the Department declines to revise §106.3(b) in the final regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble notes commenters requested clearer definitions of 'monetary damages' and constraints on the Assistant Secretary's remedial authority, but the Department retained §106.3(b) and declined to define monetary damages in the rulemaking context since the reference to 'assessment of damages' was removed.
